analysis.investment_thesis: Bajaj Electricals is a no-growth stalwart with 0.6% revenue CAGR and 2.3% earnings CAGR over 9 years, priced at a preposterous 120x trailing P/E — PEG ratio exceeds 50. There is no compelling growth story here, and negative operating margins (-2.1%) make the valuation completely indefensible by any GARP framework.
key_strengths: Bajaj brand equity is a genuine household name across India with multi-category reach (fans, appliances, lighting, grooming)
Debt dramatically reduced from ₹1,084 Cr (2020) to ₹243 Cr (2025) — balance sheet is meaningfully cleaner
Consistent positive free cash flow every year for 5 years, generating ₹318 Cr FCF in FY25
key_risks: Revenue of ₹4,826 Cr in FY25 is barely above ₹4,590 Cr in FY16 — nearly a decade of stagnation is disqualifying for any growth investor
Negative operating margin (-2.1%) on a ₹4,800 Cr revenue base signals structural cost or competitive pressure, not a temporary blip
Trailing P/E of 120x on 2.3% earnings CAGR implies PEG >50 — even the forward P/E of 28.75 requires a turnaround that hasn't been earned yet
red_flags: PEG ratio >50 using trailing earnings — the single worst metric I look at
Operating margins are negative (-2.1%) despite ₹4,826 Cr in revenue — an established consumer brand should not be losing money at the operating level
Net profit of ₹133 Cr in FY25 is essentially unchanged from ₹108 Cr in FY16 — zero compounding over 9 years
Net profit trend classified as 'contracting' with ₹131–133 Cr in FY24–25 vs ₹216 Cr peak in FY23
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From where I stand, every great investment needs a clear, simple story: "This company is growing fast, the market doesn't realize it yet, and I'm buying it cheap." Bajaj Electricals has none of that. Revenue was ₹4,590 Cr in 2016 and is ₹4,826 Cr in 2025 — that's a rounding error. Net profit of ₹133 Cr in FY25 versus ₹108 Cr in FY16 is 2.3% CAGR. I could have earned more in a savings account. This is a slow grower priced like a fast grower, which is the most dangerous combination in investing. The -2.1% operating margin is the most troubling number in this entire filing — this company sells fans and kitchen appliances to hundreds of millions of Indians, and it's losing money at the operating line.

The only honest bull case is a turnaround: the forward P/E of 28.75 implies the market expects a dramatic earnings recovery, perhaps from the EPC business exit or cost restructuring. The debt cleanup from ₹1,084 Cr to ₹243 Cr is real progress. But turnarounds are risky bets, and I need to see the turn before I buy. ROE at 7.12% against my 12% threshold, D/E at 0.85 above my 0.6 limit, and zero revenue growth for nine years make this a stock to watch only after margins turn positive and earnings sustain above ₹200 Cr for two consecutive years. At ₹391, you're paying far too much for a company that hasn't yet proven it deserves a second act.
